questions.stem: Thirty minutes after a right subclavian central venous catheter is placed at the bedside, a client becomes anxious and short of breath with sharp right chest pain. Respiratory rate is 32/min, SpO2 is 88% on 2 L/min, breath sounds are absent over the right upper chest, and the right chest is hyperresonant. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, and the trachea is midline. A confirming chest x-ray has not yet been taken. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Raise the head of the bed, give oxygen and notify the provider
Prepare for a chest x-ray and possible chest tube insertion
Flush the new central line with 20 mL of saline before using it
Start the prescribed vasopressor through the new central line
Lay the client flat to reduce the work of breathing

parameters.text: Respiratory rate, SpO2 and breath sounds
Urine output measured and recorded each hour
Fingerstick blood glucose before meals and at bedtime
Bowel sounds listened for in each of the four quadrants

rationale.correct: Pneumothorax is a known complication of subclavian and internal jugular line placement; confirm placement by x-ray before use and watch for signs of tension.

perOption.c1: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the side of a subclavian line placement point to a pneumothorax; normal blood pressure and a midline trachea suggest it is not yet under tension.
perOption.c2: Air embolism causes sudden hypotension, confusion and a mill-wheel murmur, not one-sided absent breath sounds.
perOption.c3: Blood pressure is normal and the trachea is midline, so tension has not developed yet.
perOption.c4: PE does not cause absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on one side.
perOption.a1: Supports breathing and gets the provider to the bedside.
perOption.a2: Imaging confirms it, and a chest tube may be needed.
perOption.a3: This does not address the problem, and the line's position is not yet confirmed.
perOption.a4: The line should not be used until placement is confirmed.
perOption.p1: Show whether the pneumothorax is enlarging.
perOption.p2: Falling pressure or tracheal shift signals tension pneumothorax.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client admitted with an upper GI bleed has a central line. Readings: central venous pressure 2 mm Hg, heart rate 122/min, blood pressure 92/58 mm Hg and urine output 18 mL/hr. How should the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: Fluid overload from the IV fluids that have been given since admission
Hypovolemia from blood loss, with poor filling of the heart
Right-sided heart failure that is reducing cardiac output
An expected reading after placement of a new central line

rationale.correct: CVP reflects right-heart filling (normal about 2 to 8 mm Hg); a low CVP with tachycardia and hypotension points to hypovolemia, a high CVP to overload or right heart failure.

perOption.a: Fluid overload raises CVP; a CVP of 2 is low.
perOption.b: A low CVP with tachycardia, low blood pressure and low urine output shows intravascular volume depletion.
perOption.d: These values with signs of shock are not expected.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Interpret central venous pressure.

questions.stem: A client on telemetry suddenly becomes dizzy and pale. The monitor shows P waves at 78/min and QRS complexes at 34/min with no relationship between them. Blood pressure is 74/40 mm Hg. Atropine has not helped. What should the nurse prepare for next?

options.text: Synchronized cardioversion at 100 joules
Transcutaneous pacing with pads on the chest
A dose of IV adenosine given rapidly
Starting CPR right away

rationale.correct: Symptomatic bradycardia or complete heart block that does not respond to atropine is treated with transcutaneous pacing or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion.

perOption.a: Cardioversion is for unstable tachycardias, not complete heart block.
perOption.b: Symptomatic third-degree heart block that does not respond to atropine is treated with pacing.
perOption.c: Adenosine slows conduction and is for supraventricular tachycardia.
perOption.d: The client has a pulse and blood pressure; CPR is for pulselessness.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing an adult client for a lumbar puncture. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: Supine with the head of the bed raised to 45 degrees and the knees straight
On the side with the back curved, knees drawn up and chin tucked to the chest
Prone with a pillow under the chest and arms raised above the head
Standing and leaning forward over the bedside table with the arms resting on it

rationale.correct: For lumbar puncture, place the client side-lying in a curled (fetal) position, or sitting and leaning forward over a table.

perOption.a: This position does not open the spaces between the lumbar vertebrae.
perOption.b: Curling opens the spaces between the vertebrae so the needle can enter the spinal canal.
perOption.c: Prone is not the standard bedside lumbar puncture position.
perOption.d: Standing is unsafe; sitting and leaning forward is an alternative, but not standing.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with ascites is scheduled for a bedside paracentesis. Which action should the nurse take right before the procedure?

options.text: Keep the client NPO for 12 hours before the procedure
Have the client empty the bladder right before the procedure
Place the client flat on the left side with the knees bent
Give a large glass of water to keep the client hydrated during the procedure

rationale.correct: Before paracentesis: have the client void, record weight, girth and vital signs, and position upright or semi-Fowler's.

perOption.a: Prolonged fasting is not usually required for paracentesis.
perOption.b: An empty bladder lowers the risk of puncturing it with the needle.
perOption.c: The client usually sits upright or with the head raised so fluid collects in the lower abdomen.
perOption.d: Extra fluid fills the bladder, which raises the risk of puncture.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: Three days after a bowel resection, a client has abdominal distention, no flatus for 24 hours, nausea and absent bowel sounds. The client has been receiving IV hydromorphone every 3 hours and has walked only once. Vital signs are stable, there is no fever, and the pain is diffuse and crampy rather than sharp. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Peritonitis from a leak at the join between the bowel ends
Paralytic ileus worsened by opioids and immobility
Constipation from not eating enough fiber at home
Acute appendicitis that developed after the surgery

rationale.correct: Postoperative ileus causes distention, absent bowel sounds and no flatus; opioids and immobility worsen it. Treatment includes NPO status, NG decompression if vomiting, walking and opioid-sparing analgesia.

perOption.a: Peritonitis usually causes fever, tachycardia, rigidity and severe localized pain.
perOption.b: Absent bowel sounds, distention and no flatus after bowel surgery, with stable vital signs and heavy opioid use, fit paralytic ileus.
perOption.c: Diet before surgery does not explain these postoperative findings.
perOption.d: The picture fits ileus, not appendicitis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize postoperative ileus.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews laboratory results for four clients. For each result, indicate whether it is expected for the client's situation or should be reported now.

rows.text: INR 2.6 in a client taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation (target 2 to 3)
Potassium 5.9 mEq/L in a client taking lisinopril and spironolactone
Glucose 46 mg/dL in a client on insulin who is sweating
Hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL in a client admitted for a knee replacement

rationale.correct: Interpret labs in context: in-range values and drug targets are expected; dangerous electrolyte levels and symptomatic hypoglycemia need immediate action.

perOption.r1:c1: This is within the target range.
perOption.r2:c1: Both drugs raise potassium; this level is dangerous.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: On the fourth day after an open abdominal surgery, which findings suggest a surgical site infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Increasing redness spreading 3 cm from the incision
Thick yellow drainage with an odor
A slight pink line along well-joined wound edges
A temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F) with increasing incision pain
A ridge of firm tissue under the incision
Mild itching around the incision

rationale.correct: Surgical site infection usually appears 3 to 7 days after surgery: spreading redness, purulent drainage, fever and increasing pain; a healing ridge and mild pinkness are normal.

perOption.a: Spreading redness beyond the edges suggests infection.
perOption.b: Purulent drainage is a sign of infection.
perOption.c: Mild pinkness along approximated edges is normal healing.
perOption.d: Fever and worsening pain after day 3 suggest infection.
perOption.e: A healing ridge forms normally by about day 5 to 9.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old was admitted 2 hours ago after a diving accident with a complete spinal cord injury at C6. Blood pressure is now 78/42 mm Hg, heart rate 48/min, and the skin is warm, dry and pink below the injury. There is no external bleeding, and the abdomen is soft. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Give IV fluids and prepare prescribed vasopressors
Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees to help breathing
Give a large dose of furosemide to protect the kidneys
Apply a warming blanket at a high setting to raise the heart rate

parameters.text: Pupil size and response to light once each shift
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants once a shift
Body weight measured on the same scale once a week

rationale.correct: Neurogenic shock follows injury at T6 or above: hypotension, bradycardia and warm skin. Treat with fluids, vasopressors and atropine, and watch breathing closely.

perOption.c1: Loss of sympathetic tone after a cervical injury causes hypotension, bradycardia and warm, dry skin.
perOption.c2: Bleeding causes tachycardia and cool, pale skin.
perOption.c3: Dysreflexia causes severe hypertension and occurs later, after spinal shock resolves.
perOption.c4: There is no infection source this early, and the pattern fits loss of sympathetic tone.
perOption.a1: Fluids and vasopressors restore blood pressure and spinal cord perfusion.
perOption.a2: Unopposed vagal tone slows the heart; atropine treats symptomatic bradycardia.
perOption.a3: Sitting up worsens hypotension in neurogenic shock.
perOption.a5: Warming does not treat neurogenic shock and these clients lose temperature control.
perOption.p1: Show the response to fluids, vasopressors and atropine.
perOption.p2: A C6 injury affects breathing muscles, and the injury level can rise with swelling.
perOption.p3: Not the key guide for this condition.
perOption.p5: Not relevant in the acute phase.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize and treat neurogenic shock.

questions.stem: A client with ARDS from sepsis is on a ventilator with an FiO2 of 0.8 and PEEP of 12 cm H2O. The PaO2 is still 56 mm Hg. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Lowering the PEEP to reduce pressure on the lungs
Prone positioning for long periods each day
Giving a large IV fluid bolus to improve oxygen delivery
Removing the ventilator and starting a nasal cannula at 6 L/min

rationale.correct: Refractory hypoxemia in ARDS is managed with lung-protective ventilation, PEEP, conservative fluids and prone positioning.

perOption.a: Lower PEEP would allow more alveoli to collapse and worsen hypoxemia.
perOption.b: Prone positioning improves oxygenation and survival in moderate to severe ARDS.
perOption.c: Extra fluid can worsen lung edema in ARDS.
perOption.d: The client needs more, not less, respiratory support.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Anticipate treatment for refractory hypoxemia in ARDS.

questions.stem: A client who weighs 80 kg is receiving fluid resuscitation 8 hours after a 40% total body surface area burn. Which finding best shows the fluid resuscitation is adequate?

options.text: Blood pressure of 132/84 mm Hg
Urine output of 40 to 50 mL/hr
Heart rate of 112/min that has stayed the same
Absence of thirst when the client is asked

rationale.correct: In burn resuscitation, titrate fluids to urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/hr in adults (about 1 mL/kg/hr in small children).

perOption.a: Blood pressure can stay normal while organs are underperfused.
perOption.b: In adults, urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/hr (about 40 mL/hr for 80 kg) is the main guide to burn resuscitation.
perOption.c: Tachycardia is common in burns but does not confirm adequate resuscitation.
perOption.d: Thirst is not a reliable guide.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate burn fluid resuscitation.

questions.stem: Two days after a traumatic brain injury, a client's urine output is 450 mL/hr for 3 hours. Urine specific gravity is 1.002, serum sodium is 152 mEq/L and the client is very thirsty. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Fluid restriction and an infusion of 3% saline
Desmopressin and replacement of the lost water
A loop diuretic such as furosemide to control the sodium
Insulin, since the high urine output suggests hyperglycemia

rationale.correct: Diabetes insipidus: large volumes of dilute urine, high serum sodium and thirst; treat with desmopressin and water replacement, and monitor sodium and output.

perOption.a: This treats SIADH, which causes low sodium and concentrated urine.
perOption.b: Large dilute urine output with high sodium after brain injury is diabetes insipidus; desmopressin replaces ADH.
perOption.c: Diuretics would worsen the water loss.
perOption.d: Hyperglycemia causes high specific gravity from glucose, not 1.002.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize diabetes insipidus after brain injury.

questions.stem: A client who took extended-release oxycodone was given naloxone 0.4 mg IV for a respiratory rate of 6/min. Ten minutes later the client is awake with a respiratory rate of 16/min. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Document that the overdose has resolved and plan for discharge
Keep monitoring breathing and sedation, ready to repeat naloxone
Give the client's next scheduled oxycodone dose to prevent withdrawal
Stop the close monitoring now that the client is awake and talking normally

rationale.correct: Naloxone's effect is shorter than that of many opioids, especially long-acting ones; monitor closely and expect repeat doses or an infusion.

perOption.a: Naloxone wears off in 30 to 90 minutes, before extended-release oxycodone does.
perOption.b: Respiratory depression can return as naloxone wears off; repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.
perOption.c: More opioid would worsen the toxicity.
perOption.d: Monitoring must continue for several hours.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: Review the nurse's note. Highlight the findings that are most important for deciding on emergency stroke treatment.

segments.text: slurred speech, a right facial droop and right-sided weakness
atrial fibrillation with apixaban stopped 2 weeks ago
The client lives with a spouse

rationale.correct: Time last known well, sudden focal deficits, a cardioembolic risk factor and a CT without bleeding are key to emergency stroke decisions.

perOption.s2: The time last known well sets the window for thrombolytic therapy.
perOption.s4: Sudden focal deficits suggest an acute stroke.
perOption.s6: Untreated atrial fibrillation is a likely source of an embolic stroke.
perOption.s8: Important for discharge planning, not the emergency decision.
perOption.s10: Ruling out hemorrhage is required before thrombolysis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues for acute stroke treatment.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client is most likely having {{b1}}, probably caused by {{b2}}, and is {{b3}} for thrombolytic therapy based on time.

options.text: an acute ischemic stroke in the left hemisphere
a hemorrhagic stroke
a transient ischemic attack that has already resolved
a clot from the heart related to atrial fibrillation
low blood sugar
a migraine with aura
still within the window
too late
not eligible because of the time

rationale.correct: An embolic ischemic stroke from untreated atrial fibrillation within 4.5 hours of last known well can be treated with a thrombolytic if no contraindication exists.

perOption.b1:a: Right-sided weakness and speech problems point to the left hemisphere; the CT shows no bleed.
perOption.b2:a: Stopping anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation raises embolic stroke risk.
perOption.b2:c: The history and risk factors point to a cardioembolic stroke.
perOption.b3:a: Thrombolysis can be given up to 4.5 hours after last known well; 0900 to 1015 is within the window.
perOption.b3:c: Time does not exclude this client.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze cues in acute ischemic stroke.

questions.stem: Before thrombolytic therapy, the team reviews the client's data. For each finding, indicate whether it currently prevents giving the thrombolytic.

rows.text: INR 1.1 after stopping apixaban 2 weeks ago

rationale.correct: Before thrombolysis, blood pressure must be lowered below 185/110 mm Hg; normal coagulation, platelets and glucose do not prevent treatment.

perOption.r1:c1: Blood pressure must be below 185/110 before a thrombolytic is given; it must be lowered first.
perOption.r2:c1: A normal INR and no recent anticoagulant dose do not prevent treatment.
perOption.r3:c1: A normal platelet count does not prevent treatment.
perOption.r4:c1: Glucose is within the acceptable range.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Identify barriers to thrombolytic therapy.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse anticipate before the thrombolytic is started? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lower the blood pressure below 185/110 mm Hg
Complete a baseline NIH Stroke Scale assessment
Place any needed tubes and catheters before the infusion
Give a dose of aspirin by mouth now to start clot prevention early
Keep the client NPO until a swallow screen is done
Restart the apixaban at the client's usual home dose right away

rationale.correct: Before thrombolysis: blood pressure below 185/110, baseline NIHSS, lines and tubes placed first, NPO until a swallow screen and no antithrombotic drugs.

perOption.b: A baseline score guides decisions and later comparisons.
perOption.c: Invasive lines and tubes are placed before thrombolysis when possible to reduce bleeding.
perOption.d: Antiplatelets are held for 24 hours after a thrombolytic, and the client needs a swallow screen first.
perOption.e: Stroke clients are at risk of aspiration.
perOption.f: Anticoagulants are not given before or right after thrombolysis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.educationalObjective: Prepare a client for thrombolytic therapy.

questions.stem: The provider prescribes IV labetalol 10 mg now. Ten minutes later, the blood pressure is 178/104 mm Hg and the heart rate is 88/min. The thrombolytic is ready. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait 30 minutes to make sure the blood pressure stays down before starting
Start the thrombolytic and check the blood pressure often
Give a second dose of labetalol to bring the pressure below 140/90 first
Hold the thrombolytic, since the blood pressure was high on arrival

rationale.correct: Once blood pressure is below 185/110, start the thrombolytic and keep the pressure below 180/105 with frequent checks for 24 hours.

perOption.a: Delay reduces the benefit of thrombolysis; the target has been reached.
perOption.b: The pressure is now below 185/110; during and after treatment it must stay below 180/105 with frequent checks.
perOption.c: Lowering pressure too far can reduce brain perfusion.
perOption.d: Treated blood pressure that meets the target does not prevent thrombolysis.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Two hours after the thrombolytic infusion, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or needs immediate action.

rows.text: Speech clearer and right hand grip stronger

rationale.correct: After thrombolysis, improving deficits and a falling NIHSS show response; a new headache, vomiting or neurological decline suggests hemorrhage and needs immediate action.

perOption.r3:c1: These may signal bleeding in the brain.
perOption.r3:c2: Stop any infusion and notify the provider now.
perOption.r4:c1: This is within the post-thrombolytic limit of 180/105.

rationale.correct: Severe hypoxemia, worsening blood gases and pink frothy sputum show acute pulmonary edema needing immediate treatment.

perOption.r2: Hypoxemia with rising CO2 shows respiratory failure is developing.
perOption.r3: Normal; this matters before diuresis but is not urgent.
perOption.r4: Pink frothy sputum signals fluid flooding the alveoli.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of acute pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client is having {{b1}}, triggered by {{b2}}.

options.text: acute pulmonary edema from decompensated heart failure
pneumonia
an asthma attack
a high-sodium meal and a missed diuretic dose
too much exercise during the day
a new allergy to a medication

rationale.correct: Dietary sodium and missed diuretics are common triggers of acute decompensated heart failure.

perOption.b1:a: Sudden dyspnea, crackles, pink frothy sputum and hypoxemia in a client with a low ejection fraction fit pulmonary edema.
perOption.b1:b: There is no fever, and the onset is sudden with frothy sputum.
perOption.b1:c: Crackles and pink sputum point to fluid, not bronchospasm.
perOption.b2:a: Sodium and fluid retention without the diuretic overwhelm the weak heart.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze the trigger of acute pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Sit the client upright and start oxygen or BiPAP as prescribed
Lay the client flat in bed so they can rest and conserve energy
Give a 500 mL IV fluid bolus to slow the client's fast heart rate
Encourage the client to drink a full glass of water to loosen the sputum

parameters.text: Oxygen saturation and work of breathing
Fingerstick blood glucose before meals and at bedtime
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants once a shift
Pupil size and reaction to light each shift

rationale.correct: Acute pulmonary edema: upright position, oxygen or noninvasive ventilation, IV diuretics and nitrates, with close monitoring of oxygenation, urine output and blood pressure.

perOption.c1: Gasping, crackles, pink frothy sputum and hypoxemia show fluid in the alveoli.
perOption.c2: PE does not cause crackles throughout the lungs with frothy sputum.
perOption.c3: The findings fit fluid overload, not bronchospasm.
perOption.c4: Anxiety does not cause hypoxemia and crackles.
perOption.a1: Upright positioning reduces venous return, and oxygen or BiPAP improves oxygenation.
perOption.a2: Diuresis removes fluid and nitrates reduce preload and afterload.
perOption.a3: Lying flat increases venous return and worsens dyspnea.
perOption.p2: Show the response to diuretics and nitrates and guard against hypotension.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize care for acute pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: The provider prescribes noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (BiPAP). Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fit the mask snugly and check for air leaks
Keep the head of the bed raised
Watch for worsening drowsiness or inability to protect the airway
Give the client a full meal while the mask is on
Check the skin on the bridge of the nose for pressure injury

rationale.correct: BiPAP care: good mask fit, upright position, close watch for failure (drowsiness, rising CO2), no eating with the mask on and skin protection.

perOption.a: A good seal is needed for effective pressure.
perOption.b: Upright position helps breathing and lowers aspiration risk.
perOption.c: These mean BiPAP is failing and intubation may be needed.
perOption.d: Eating with the mask on risks aspiration.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Provide care during noninvasive ventilation.

questions.stem: The client is started on a nitroglycerin infusion. Thirty minutes later the blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg, and the client feels lightheaded. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Increase the nitroglycerin rate to reduce the preload further
Stop or reduce the nitroglycerin per protocol and notify the provider
Lay the client completely flat with the legs raised and continue the infusion as it is
Give a 1 L IV fluid bolus to raise the blood pressure

rationale.correct: Titrate nitroglycerin to blood pressure; with hypotension, stop or reduce it per protocol and notify the provider.

perOption.a: A higher rate would worsen hypotension.
perOption.b: Hypotension is a common effect of nitroglycerin; stopping or reducing it usually restores the pressure quickly.
perOption.c: The infusion must be adjusted, and lying flat may worsen the pulmonary edema.
perOption.d: A large fluid bolus would worsen pulmonary edema.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: At 0800, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or needs follow-up.

rows.text: SpO2 94% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula
Crackles only at the lung bases

rationale.correct: Better oxygenation, strong diuresis and fewer crackles show response; low potassium after diuresis needs replacement.

perOption.r1:c1: Oxygenation has improved enough to stop BiPAP.
perOption.r3:c1: Fluid in the lungs has decreased.
perOption.r4:c1: Diuresis has lowered potassium, raising dysrhythmia risk.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate the response to treatment of pulmonary edema.

caseStudies.title: Acute ischemic stroke in the thrombolytic window

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 1015
exhibits.body: A 68-year-old client was last known well at 0900 when they spoke normally with a neighbor. At 0945 the spouse found the client with slurred speech, a right facial droop and weakness of the right arm and leg. History: hypertension, atrial fibrillation (stopped apixaban 2 weeks ago because of cost) and type 2 diabetes. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows no bleeding.

caseStudies.title: Acute pulmonary edema in heart failure

exhibits.title: Medical unit, 0330
exhibits.body: A 72-year-old client with heart failure (ejection fraction 25%) wakes up gasping and sits on the edge of the bed. The client is anxious, sweating and coughing up frothy pink sputum. Crackles are heard throughout both lungs. The client says they ate a large ham dinner and skipped the evening furosemide dose.
